claims.text: This is a tonkatsu specialist: pork is dredged in wheat flour and panko breadcrumbs, then deep-fried. It is not gluten-free and not safe for celiac diners. The breading is wheat-based and the same fryer is used for all breaded items, so cross-contamination of oil is expected.
Mixed-fry plates pair the cutlet with breaded seafood (such as kisu/whiting) cooked in the same oil, so there is no separate gluten-free frying.

Tonkatsu is served with tonkatsu sauce and a teishoku set (miso soup, soy-based seasonings). Most Japanese soy sauce and tonkatsu sauce contain wheat, so these are not safe for celiac or strict gluten-free diners.

The menu is built around deep-fried pork cutlets, with miso soup and dashi-based accompaniments. There are no vegan or vegetarian options indicated, and the shared fryer is used exclusively for breaded animal products.

No allergen information is published and no reports describe how staff handle allergy requests. With only an older couple running a small, no-reservation counter, anyone with a serious allergy should call ahead to confirm: 075-703-4116.

The kitchen is consistently praised as exceptionally clean and meticulous, with each cutlet prepared and fried fresh to order — good for general food hygiene, though not a substitute for allergen control.

This is a classic Showa kissaten whose core menu is built on wheat bread: egg sandwiches, toast, and morning sets. There is no gluten-free menu, no documented dedicated gluten-free prep, and shared surfaces and a small kitchen make cross-contact likely. Treat as unsuitable for strict gluten avoidance.
Signature items center on white bread (the tamago sando on fluffy bread, toast with the morning set), so wheat is unavoidable in the headline dishes.

No menu or source documents the soy sauce or seasonings used. Yoshoku items such as the hamburger steak and beef curry, plus the ketchup-touched egg sandwich, commonly involve sauces; most Japanese soy sauce contains wheat, so assume wheat-containing seasonings unless staff confirm otherwise.

No vegan options or accommodations are documented. The kitchen is egg-, dairy-, and meat-heavy (egg sandwiches, fried eggs on the morning set and hamburger steak, coffee with milk), so cross-contact with animal products is likely across shared prep surfaces and cookware.

name: 京お好み 鉄平 (Kyo Okonomi Teppei)

claims.text: This is not a celiac-safe restaurant. Okonomiyaki, betayaki, and negiyaki are all built on wheat-flour batters and cooked on a single shared teppan (griddle) alongside other wheat-based items, so flour and batter cross-contact on the cooking surface is essentially unavoidable. No gluten-free preparation or dedicated cooking area is documented.

Okonomiyaki is typically finished with a soy-based okonomiyaki sauce, and the batter is usually mixed with dashi; most Japanese soy sauce and okonomiyaki sauce contain wheat, adding another gluten source beyond the flour batter itself.

No vegan or vegetarian options are documented. Okonomiyaki batter is generally bound with egg and made with dashi (commonly fish/bonito based), the griddle is shared with meat and seafood, and dishes are typically topped with bonito flakes, so cross-contact with animal products is expected.

This is a from-scratch Showa-era yoshoku diner whose core dishes are built on wheat: hamburg steak with a flour-thickened demi-glace, hand-breaded fried shrimp and white-fish fry (the panko is reportedly made in-house), Napolitan spaghetti, pork piccata and ketchup-rice omurice. Gluten is structural to the menu, not an occasional ingredient.

Cooking happens in a tiny kitchen serving roughly 6 counter seats, where one chef prepares everything by hand. With breaded fry, floured sauces and pasta all made in the same small space, cross-contact with wheat is effectively unavoidable. There is no gluten-free menu or allergen protocol indicated, so this place should be considered unsafe for anyone with celiac disease.

As a Japanese kitchen, sauces and seasonings here are very likely to include soy sauce and other wheat-containing condiments; most standard Japanese soy sauce is brewed with wheat. No wheat-free soy alternative is mentioned anywhere, so soy-based seasonings should be assumed to contain gluten.

The menu centers on meat, egg, shrimp and fish (hamburg steak, omelets/omurice, fried shrimp, white-fish fry, piccata), and Japanese yoshoku cooking typically relies on meat-based demi-glace and dashi. There is no vegan option indicated, and shared pans, oil and surfaces make animal-product cross-contact likely.

No allergen handling, ingredient labeling or accommodation for dietary restrictions is documented in any available source. This is a traditional one-cook, husband-and-wife diner rather than an allergy-aware kitchen, so anyone with a serious allergy or celiac disease should confirm directly with the owners before ordering, and likely look elsewhere.

Nearly everything is made fresh and by hand each morning, so the owners know exactly what goes into their dishes; a direct, in-person conversation with them about ingredients is likely to get an honest, informed answer even though no formal allergen system exists.
Not celiac-safe. The core product is handmade wheat udon, so wheat and gluten are central to nearly every dish and cross-contamination is unavoidable in a noodle-focused kitchen.
Tempura (shrimp and chicken) is a signature offering, which adds wheat-flour batter and likely shared frying oil to the gluten picture.
Dishes use soy-based seasonings, and most Japanese soy sauce contains wheat — an additional gluten source beyond the noodles themselves.
Not vegan-friendly. The signature broth is built from bonito and niboshi (dried small fish) alongside kombu, so dashi-based dishes contain fish. Tempura includes shrimp and chicken.
No specific allergy-handling reports were found in available sources. Diners with allergies should confirm directly with the shop before ordering.

This is not a celiac-safe restaurant. The core product is hand-stretched wheat-flour gyoza, and the menu also includes ramen, fried rice, and Tianjin rice, all of which involve wheat and/or soy. No gluten-free accommodation is documented, and with hand-made wheat skins prepared daily in a small open kitchen, airborne flour and shared surfaces make cross-contamination effectively unavoidable.

The gyoza filling includes glass noodles and the skins are wheat; the kitchen is a small counter operation where the same surfaces and grill are used for all dishes, so flour cross-contact should be assumed.

Gyoza here are served with standard dipping condiments including a soy/vinegar-style dip and a house miso-based sauce. Most Japanese soy sauce contains wheat, and miso may also contain barley or wheat, so the dipping sauces are not gluten-free.

Not suitable for vegans. The gyoza filling contains ground meat, the menu features egg dishes (Tianjin rice, egg soup) and meat-based Chinese dishes, and there are no documented vegan options. Even the vegetable-forward gyoza contain meat and are cooked on a shared grill.

This is a toast- and cake-centric café whose signature items are wheat-based (butter toast, the all-day morning plate, and cakes), prepared in a shared kitchen. No gluten-free menu or dedicated handling is documented, so wheat exposure should be assumed throughout. Not celiac-safe.

No specific information on soy sauce was found in the sources. The salad-topped curry on the menu would conventionally be roux-thickened (wheat); confirm ingredients directly if you are gluten-sensitive.

No vegan menu or handling is documented. Core offerings center on butter toast, bacon, eggs, yogurt, café au lait, and butter/dairy-style cakes, so animal products are pervasive and cross-contact with vegan items cannot be assumed avoided. Note the kinako cake contains soybean flour but other cakes/toast are not vegan.

This is a tempura specialty house, so the core of every course is wheat-flour batter deep-fried in shared oil. The house 'Kyoboshi-style' coating is described as essentially just flour and water, applied very thin, but it is still wheat-based. It is not celiac-safe.
All pieces are fried in the same oil, so even non-battered items would share frying oil with wheat batter. There is no indication of a dedicated gluten-free fryer.

Tempura here is finished with house-blended salt, grated daikon, and lemon juice rather than a soy-based tentsuyu, so the tempura course itself avoids dipping sauce. However, an omakase-style Japanese course of this type commonly includes soy- and dashi-based elements, and most Japanese soy sauce contains wheat. Confirm with the kitchen before relying on this.

No vegan or vegetarian options are documented in any source. The batter is egg-free, but the kitchen serves a fixed tempura omakase fried in shared oil with seafood, so cross-contact with animal ingredients is likely. Vegan status should be confirmed directly with the restaurant.

No information was found in available sources about how staff handle allergy or dietary requests. As a small counter serving a fixed course, customization is likely limited, so contact the restaurant in advance to discuss any needs.
The batter is made without eggs, which is helpful for diners with an egg allergy (though shared frying oil and seafood mean cross-contact cannot be ruled out).

The tempura is dressed only with house salt, grated daikon, and lemon juice rather than a flour-thickened or soy-based dipping sauce, so the fried pieces themselves carry no added soy or sauce-borne wheat.
